transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-12
Time: 3:00 PM PT
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Reddy (Montvue Eng Mgr), Tomás Alvarez (Montvue SRE), Lena Park (Product), Jordan Wu (Security)

Summary: quick console walkthrough focused on request forensics, request logs, KV-cache behavior and a potential POC to repro occasional 500s they see. Customer wants to understand how Redwood surfaces request traces, links to logs and how cache fallbacks are visible.

Topics: console request inspector, request playback, KV cache hit/miss instrumentation, error triage workflow, security/audit logs, POC scope and timeline

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone good afternoon, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, im the AE on the account, and with me is Ethan our solutions engineer.
[00:10] Ethan: Hi all, hey Priya Tomás, quick agenda: we'll show the Console request inspector, how traces are surfaced, walk through a sample 500 error and then talk KV-cache fallbacks and telemetry.
[00:21] Priya: Thanks, we appreciate it. We've been seeing intermittent 500s when requests are long and sometimes the responses are garbled, so trying to figure out if it's our payload, tokenization, or something in the serving path.
[00:34] Tomás: Also we need to know if Redwood can give us request-level audit logs for HIPAA control mapping, and how long those are retained.
[00:45] Maya: Great points, we'll cover retention, RBAC audit hooks, and also show the trace -> log linkage in the console. Quick note: I'll share the deck and the SOC2 / security pack after the call.
[01:05] Ethan: Alright jumping into the console. Sorry spelling: this is Redwood Console (we sometimes see it auto-transcribed as Red wood Consoel). On the main Requests tab you can search by request-id, model, route, and time range.
[01:26] Ethan: Here's an example request we repro'd earlier, request-id 9f3a2b. You can see latency, token counts, and an initial error status 500. The console shows a waterfall timeline with upstream steps and the serving node that returned the error.
[01:47] Lena: Is the waterfall showing client-side vs server-side timing? Can we distinguish network egress time?
[01:56] Ethan: Yes, you get breakdowns: client -> edge -> serving runtime -> model inference. Network egress is approximated, we also surface region and node id so you can correlate with your infra logs.
[02:18] Tomás: When KV cache is enabled, does the console show cache hit rates per request or per prefix? We've seen weird cold-starts.
[02:28] Ethan: Good question. We have per-request cache meta: hit/miss, hit_probability, ttl remaining. In the request inspector you'll see a "KV-cache" section that lists keys probed and which were hits. Not every key is enumerated for PII reasons but we give hashes + reason codes.
[02:47] Priya: Are those hashes reversible? We need to be sure about PHI.
[02:53] Jordan: yeah security question — do hashes or cache keys leak any part of content?
[02:57] Ethan: Short answer: no reversible tokens in the UI. We show salted hashes and obfuscated prefixes. For HIPAA we'd recommend private deployment or dedicated pools and KMS integrations, we provide HSM/KMS options for key management.
[03:20] Maya: I'll attach the private deployment security sheet, also the retention windows we support for audit logs.
[03:28] Ethan: Back to the trace: here's a trace span that shows a fallback case — the runtime attempted a KV-cache lookup, missed, then tried a prefix fetch from the model and then fell back to a quantized variant due to load. The console notes the fallback reason code: "capacity:quantized-fallback"
[03:50] Priya: Can we get raw trace export? Our incident toolchain ingests OpenTelemetry.
[03:56] Ethan: Yes, you can export traces as OTLP or JSON. We also support a one-click export to S3 for longer retention. I can demo export afterwards.
[04:12] Tomás: The 500 we see in prod spikes around 2am PT, any way to find a pattern by input size or by model?
[04:20] Ethan: The requests table supports aggregations and facet by model, seq length, tokens_in and tokens_out. You can create a saved view that filters errors and time windows, then we can query by payload length buckets.
[04:40] Maya: we'll follow up with a quick sample query and a small spreadsheet to map their spike times.
[04:50] Priya: Do you have an example of the error stack? Their errors are sometimes a generic 500 with no useful stack.
[04:57] Ethan: In the request detail we show the runtime error message, model stderr snippet if present, and recent kernel logs (redacted). It's not always a full stack trace — sometimes it's a model OOM and we show OOM metadata.
[05:15] Ethan: I'm going to play a recorded request now (request playback). Playback replays the same request through the serving runtime for debugging, but only in a sandboxed non-production replay mode; it won't count against production quota.
[05:34] Tomás: Important — can we replay with our own headers and IP mask to mimic production?
[05:40] Ethan: Yes you can override headers, environment flags, and you can toggle KV-cache on/off during replay. This is how you can reproduce cache cold-start issues.
[05:58] Priya: When you toggle cache off, will the model behavior change because of missing context?
[06:04] Ethan: It might. We'll record both runs and diff token outputs, response time, and any fallback warnings.
[06:17] Lena: How does Redwood show degraded quality after quantized fallback? Is there a signal?
[06:22] Ethan: We have a "quality delta" metric: perplexity proxy and embedding-similarity vs the pre-quant model. If you run evaluation prompts (we can attach a small eval suite) we'll show regression metrics per model variant.
[06:41] Jordan: For audit purposes, does the console capture who initiated a replay? We need traceability for compliance.
[06:47] Ethan: Yes, audit log records username, role, request-id, and timestamps. The audit log can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[06:58] Tomás: What's the retention default for request logs? 30 days?
[07:03] Maya: Hosted default is 30 days, Dedicated can be configured to longer, and Private you control retention entirely. We'll put exact numbers in the security pack.
[07:20] Priya: Ok show us an example KV miss chain.
[07:26] Ethan: Sure. Loading request 9f3a2b: KV-cache probe list shows 3 prefixes probed, first two misses, third hit but TTL expired so treated as miss. The console returns reason codes: miss-cold, miss-ttl-expired. Then runtime falls back to prefix fetch which took 280ms, then model started streaming. But then model returned inconsistent tokens and server flagged as 500 due to tokenization exception.
[07:55] Priya: Tokenization exception? We send UTF-8 and some emojis. Could that be it?
[08:02] Ethan: Emojis can increase token count unpredictably; our tokenizer generally handles unicode but corner cases exist. We'll capture the raw input slice in the trace export as redacted text.
[08:18] Tomás: Could a quantized model variant change tokenization boundaries?
[08:22] Ethan: Not the tokenizer—token boundaries are model-agnostic. But quantized runtimes sometimes have different error thresholds and can surface different runtime errors.
[08:36] Maya: quick poll — how critical is avoiding any fallback for you? Priya?
[08:40] Priya: Ideally no fallback for latency sensitive flows, for batch non-interactive it's fine.
[08:46] Lena: For our summarization pipeline fallback leads to quality drop and downstream wrong metadata. So minimizing fallback hits is priority.
[08:57] Ethan: We recommend a hybrid: hot-path models pinned to dedicated capacity, with autoscaling and higher batch/slot quotas; cold paths go to quantized cheaper pools. The console can define routing policies per route.
[09:12] Tomás: Can we pin by client-id or route tag?
[09:15] Ethan: Yes by route, customer tag, or header. We can demo routing policies later.
[09:25] Priya: About cost — if we pin to dedicated for hot paths what's the overhead?
[09:30] Maya: We'll send a cost breakdown sample for your traffic patterns. But generally dedicated has a flat reserved hourly + utilization. We'll include suggested commit levels.
[09:45] Ethan: Back to the playback: I'm toggling cache off now and re-running. Playback shows the exact token stream and the model's stderr snippet. You can see that with cache off the inference time increased by 220ms and the response completed cleanly in this replay.
[10:09] Priya: So in replay it worked, but in prod it fails — could that be due to node/region differences?
[10:16] Ethan: Exactly. The original failure happened in eu-west-1 node-14 during a transient kernel assert. The trace links to node logs and an internal incident tag. We can surface node health over time aggregated in the console.
[10:32] Jordan: For us we need to prove to auditors that patient data never leaves the VPC, is that possible with Redwood?
[10:39] Maya: Yes with Private deployment or VPC-backed Private control plane, ingress and egress can be controlled. For hosted we offer dedicated capacity with VPC peering and encryption in transit, but pure air-gapped on-prem is available for enterprise deals.
[10:57] Tomás: If we do a POC, what's minimal scope to reproduce our 500 spikes?
[11:03] Ethan: Minimal POC: 1) sample traffic capture for the spike window (2–3 logs), 2) one model route pinned, 3) reproduce via playback with cache toggles and with their headers, 4) we'll run a 48-hour capture to surface patterns.
[11:20] Priya: Timeline wise we want initial POC in two weeks.
[11:24] Maya: Sounds good — we'll aim for kickoff week of May 25th.
[11:30] Ethan: I'll note required access: a read-only S3 with logs or a request export, and service account to run a few replays.
[11:39] Tomás: We can provide logs and a service account.
[11:43] Priya: Any red flags for PHI in the traces?
[11:47] Jordan: We need to ensure traces are redacted and that no PHI stored in cache keys.
[11:52] Ethan: We'll recommend using salted hashing and opting into PII redaction. Also for production PHI we recommend Private deployment + KMS.
[12:03] Lena: Can you show how the console surfaces anomalies across routes?
[12:08] Ethan: Sure — in the Analytics pane we have anomaly detection based on error rate, latency z-score and quality drift. It surfaces correlated signals like a sudden KV miss rate spike.
[12:26] Priya: Does anomaly detection require us to send labels or ground truth?
[12:30] Ethan: No, it works unsupervised but you can add eval sets to improve sensitivity.
[12:40] Maya: small note on integrations: we ship Slack/PagerDuty hooks and can forward alerts to your ops pipeline.
[12:49] Tomás: For the POC can we get a cost estimate for a week-long dedicated pool to pin hot routes?
[12:55] Maya: yes will include in the pricing doc.
[13:00] Ethan: I'm going to open a secondary view: request timeline rolled up by hour to show the 2am spike pattern. You can see most 500s cluster in the 02:00–03:00 window and correlate with background batch jobs.
[13:22] Priya: We do have maintenance jobs at 2am, could be interference.
[13:28] Tomás: Could autoscaling backoff cause fallback to quantized models?
[13:33] Ethan: Yes when autoscaler crosses thresholds it can re-route to lower tier variants; there are policies to avoid this for specified routes.
[13:42] Priya: How easy is it to lock a route to not fallback?
[13:46] Ethan: In routing policies you can set "no-fallback" and it will either queue or reject if capacity isn't available depending on policy.
[13:56] Jordan: For our compliance we prefer reject over silent fallback.
[13:59] Maya: totally understood we'll mark that in the POC requirements.
[14:05] Ethan: Switching to logs: request logs include request payload hash, sanitized prompt snippets, and a link to the trace. You can also click through to the export JSON which includes all spans.
[14:20] Priya: Could you share an example export link?
[14:24] Ethan: I'll paste one in chat after the call — example: https://s3.redwood-internal.example/exports/9f3a2b.json (note: placeholder)
[14:37] Tomás: We need SSO/SAML for RBAC.
[14:41] Maya: Redwood supports SAML, SCIM for user provisioning, and custom RBAC roles. We'll include the SSO setup doc in the follow-up.
[14:52] Priya: Any notes on encryption at rest for caches?
[14:55] Ethan: KV stores can be encrypted with customer KMS keys on Dedicated/Private. For hosted we use provider-managed encryption but can integrate customer KMS for dedicated.
[15:09] Maya: Ok quick recap — deliverables: security pack + SOC2 matrix (Maya), cost/pricing sample (Maya), KV-cache benchmark with their payload (Ethan), POC kickoff scheduling (Maya + Montvue), and sample trace export (Ethan).
[15:29] Priya: That covers it. Thanks for walking through the console details.
[15:32] Tomás: We'll prepare logs and service account for the replay.
[15:36] Maya: Great — I'll send notes and deck by EOD. Expect the security pack by Friday.
[15:41] Lena: Thanks everyone.
[15:44] Ethan: Thanks all, end call.
